content.summary_of_the_paper: HSVC is a transformer model for predicting vulnerability label on code. It is distilled from a set of TextCNN models trained on sub-groups of vulnerability labels so that the class imbalance problem is mitigated. The grouping is designed using domain knowledge of CWE categories. HSVC is evaluated on the Big-Vul dataset and compared against vulnerability detection models, finetuned models and grouping methods used with CodeBERT.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
* Vulnerability detection is a practically important problem and class imbalance is a real issue.
* The paper is well executed with comparison against multiple baselines.

Weaknesses
* Limited novelty: The paper makes a neat observation about grouping of labels by vulnerability categories using domain knowledge. This is the main contribution. The distillation setup is based on the DeIT approach.
* Non-vulnerable code: The real class imbalance in vulnerability detection is between vulnerable vs. non-vulnerable code with non-vulnerable code far outnumbering vulnerable cases. The authors discard non-vulnerable examples and focus on identifying type of vulnerability for code that is known to have a vulnerability. I find this setup impractical. A more useful case is when a label saying "not vulnerable" is included and false positives are minimized.
* Limited evaluation: While the authors have considered appropriate baselines, I find it unsatisfactory that they have only considered a single split with 10% of the labeled data as their test set. Why not evaluate on all of the data (8K examples) and report results on the entire set? This is particularly important because several baselines have very close performance to that of HSVC.
* Generality: The authors use the Big-Vul dataset. CVEFixes is another popular dataset. Why is it not included? Is the domain-specific grouping applicable to it?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The writing quality and clarity of the paper are quite good. The contribution is simple and not particularly novel. I am happy to see that the authors provide a link to their repo.
content.summary_of_the_review: A neat idea and well-presented work. Addressing the weaknesses listed above can improve the paper substantially.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper: To tackle the problem of imbalanced software vulnerabilities classification, this paper proposes to split the whole distribution into more balanced sub-distributions based on the CWE abstract types and distill knowledge from multiple learned experts to build a unified classification model. Specifically, they learn TextCNN teachers on each of the sub-distribution respectively and then build a student model based on transformer through hierarchical knowledge distillation. Their method is evaluated on a real-world dataset containing 8636 vulnerability types and the results outperformed other baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: The research problem of multi-class vulnerability classification is interesting and the paper is well-written and easy to understand.
Weakness: 
(1)	The application of the research problem is not promising. Binary vulnerability classification is widely researched with the importance of noticing engineers of potential security risks. But vulnerability types are usually project-dependent, multi-class vulnerability classification is of limited significance.
(2)	The novelty of the proposed method is marginal. The proposed method shares similar idea with existing works like LFME, which is to split long-tailed distribution into multiple more balanced sub-distributions to learn an expert model on each subset, and then distill knowledge from all experts to build an unified student model.
(3)	The rationale behind some technique design is weak. While the authors claim the data division methods based on label frequencies in previous approaches is not optimal for the vulnerability classification task, how the proposed data division strategy alleviates the limitation is not well clarified and explained, which further weakens the reasonability of the method.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Quality: Weak. The significance of the work is not well demonstrated.
Clarity: Good. The writing of the paper is good and clearly shows the proposed method.
Originality: Weak. The novelty is marginal and low.
content.summary_of_the_review: While this paper attempts to handle with the long-tail problem in vulnerability classification, the proposed method is mainly based on existing long-tail learning techniques with slight modification of adopting a different data division approach. The rationale behind the effectiveness of grouping source codes by CWE abstract types is not well clarified, which sheds little light on how this long-tailed problem different from others. Overall, the simple application of existing technique is lack of novelty and significance.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a hierarchical distillation approach for vulnerability classification, where the model is required to predict the CWE-ID given the input vulnerable source code. One challenge of this problem is that the label distribution is highly imbalanced. To mitigate this issue, the approach first groups CWE-IDs based on CWE abstract types, so that each group has a more balanced label distribution compared to the entire label set. Afterward, they train a shared TextCNN teacher model with different classification heads to classify labels within each group. Finally, they train a Transformer-based student model to perform classification with the full label set given the teacher model. They evaluate their approach on a subset of Fan et al.'s benchmark including vulnerable source code only, and compare their approach to multiple baseline models for vulnerability classification, as well as learning approaches to deal with label imbalance. Empirical results show that their approach outperforms the baselines and improves upon Transformer-based models that are directly trained on the dataset without knowledge distillation.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. This work proposes a practical solution to vulnerability classification problem. The approach leverages the hierarchy of the CWE labels for training teacher models, which is shown to be more effective than grouping based on the label distribution only.

2. The authors present a pretty comprehensive comparison to different types of baseline models for vulnerability classification and different training approaches. The ablation studies also clearly show the effectiveness of different design choices.

3. The source code is provided in the submission.

Weaknesses:

1. The approach is not completely novel. Knowledge distillation is not a new approach, and the modifications developed in this work are specialized for the vulnerability classification problem. Also, leveraging the Transformer architecture and hierarchy of the CWE labels for prediction is not entirely new, as discussed in the introduction section.

2. Table 6 is a bit unclear. The accuracies in this table are much higher than the student models, and I wonder how they are calculated.

3. This is more of a question, do Table 6 results indicate an empirical upper bound of the prediction performance on the dataset, or it might require a larger or better model architecture for the teacher model? I wonder whether the two teacher models make the same wrong predictions, or their accuracies just happen to be the same.

4. For teacher models, what is the breakdown accuracy of each category?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper writing is generally clear, and the proposed approach is executed well.

The approach is not entirely new. However, it is a good adaptation of methods proposed for other machine learning applications, and it appropriately leverages some properties of the vulnerability classification problem.

The source code is already provided in the submission for reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review: This work proposes an effective solution for vulnerability classification. The proposed approach is not entirely new. However, it is a good adaptation of methods proposed for other machine learning applications, and it appropriately leverages some properties of the vulnerability classification problem. Therefore, I lean towards accepting this paper.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper describes a strategy for code classification in a "long-tailed" setting, where there is considerable imbalance in the distribution of class labels. The authors propose to group these labels into sub-categories such that there is less class imbalance within each sub-category, and examples in each sub-category are more similar.

They then train individual Text-CNN models (sub-models) on each sub-category, and *distill* the knowledge from each of the sub-models into one single transformer model. They then show that this transformer model performs better on the classification task as compared to training a transformer model from scratch on all labels. They also compare this approach to other techniques for dealing with imbalanced datasets.

**Problem setting**

This paper applies this technique to solve the problem of software vulnerability classification. Given a piece of code, we want to assign it a "CVE-ID". Each CVE-ID is also associated with an abstract type, thus forming a two-level hierarchy of labels. The abstract types form the sub-categories.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**

* Software Vulnerability Classification is an important problem to solve because it helps engineers prioritize which one to work on.

* Grouping by abstract CVE type seems to work well.

* Evaluation is thorough and covers all bases.

**Weaknesses**

I have some comments on originality/novelty, as well as clarity/organization. Please see below.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity/Quality:**

I have some issues with some of the language/grammar used in the paper. Here are some that caught my attention:

* First sentence of the abstract - "Software vulnerabilities have diverse... *attacks*, ..."? Not sure if that makes sense. Maybe you meant "diverse attack patterns", or something along those lines?

* Section 3.2.3, first sentence - "At this outset, we impress upon...".

* Section 3.2.3, second sentence - "To simplify the context, in the sequel, we present the technicality..."

* Start of Section 3.1 - "Assuming we have a source code data..." - should be "Assume we have...".

Comments on flow/organization:

* In the introduction (second paragraph, Page 2), you refer *forward* to Table 4 and Table 2, which I find slightly odd. It would be better, in my opinion, to just say "As we show in this paper..."

* "Two special tokens, [cls] and [sep], are added during tokenization..." - you describe what `[cls]` is, but you don't say what `[sep]` is.

* Section 4.4.2 (Ablation Study) - comparison with other models shouldn't be part of an ablation study! An ablation study is just to evaluate the effect of ablating (removing) different components of your model to evaluate your design choices.

**Originality/Novelty:**

In terms of the technique, this paper is essentially a combination of two existing papers - Xiang et al. (2020) [1], and Touvron et al. (2021) [2].

* Xiang et al. (2020) apply hierarchical distillation based on class label distribution for a *vision* problem.
* Touvron et al. (2021) apply distillation to transformer models by using classification and distillation tokens. Their hard/soft objectives are identical to this paper.

In light of these prior works, the only technical novelty in this paper is the grouping strategy: grouping by CVE abstract types seems to perform better than the grouping in Xiang et al. (2020). This is very specific to the Software Vulnerability Classification (SVC) problem. Therefore, it is my opinion that this paper is an interesting *application*, but not a new *technique*. This might be better suited to a conference that focuses on software/security. Unfortunately, I cannot give actionable feedback on how to address this concern without changing the character/focus of the paper entirely.

The problem of choosing the best grouping strategy is non-trivial and evidently makes a not-insignificant difference to the performance of the distilled model. I think that this is an interesting direction of research. Could we train a "meta" model to form these groups automatically? Could we use some heuristics? This would definitely be an important technical contribution.

**Reproducibility:**

I appreciate that the authors have made their code public. It seems simple enough to set up and run (judging from the instructions), however I did not attempt to run it.

[1] Xiang, Liuyu, Guiguang Ding, and Jungong Han. "Learning from multiple experts: Self-paced knowledge distillation for long-tailed classification." European Conference on Computer Vision. Springer, Cham, 2020.

[2] Touvron, Hugo, et al. "Training data-efficient image transformers & distillation through attention." International Conference on Machine Learning. PMLR, 2021.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper presents a technique for hierarchical knowledge distillation in transformer models for software vulnerability classification. This is an interesting application, but I believe that the technical novelty of this paper is limited in the context of prior work. I therefore do not recommend acceptance.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
